practice: In a database service project you own, create two test users and a table of private notes, then reason through which rows each user and an anonymous visitor should be able to read.
Read the documentation on row-level security in your chosen database and write a plain-English policy for each table in a small sample app you control.
Review the network traffic of your own web app in browser developer tools and list which keys and endpoints a visitor can see.
Work through an intentionally vulnerable web lab on broken access control and note which checks were missing.
Draft a short pre-launch checklist for permissions and user separation for an app you are building.

questions.answer: They used Common Crawl web archive data to identify 159,041 Lovable projects, then narrowed to the 34,545 that used Supabase.
questions.question: How did the researchers find the projects to examine?

questions.answer: Email addresses can be public contact details or test data, and records without emails were missed, so the figure is only a proxy.
questions.question: Why is 30% not a confirmed leak rate?

questions.answer: Access-control mistakes in database integrations, where data is readable without a login or without separation between users.
questions.question: What is the underlying root cause of the exposure?

questions.answer: Lovable's terms put application security and data handling on the customer, although marketing implies little technical skill is needed.
questions.question: Who bears responsibility according to the report?

questions.answer: Review permissions and account separation, repeat after major changes, and get a professional assessment instead of relying only on automated checks.
questions.question: What do the authors recommend before using real customer data?

items.summary:
Researchers at Crissy Field studied 159,041 projects built with the AI app builder Lovable, found through Common Crawl archive data from December 2025 to September 2026. Of these, 34,545 used Supabase as the database. They checked which sites sent database records to any visitor on first page load, with no login. That gave 24,664 sites. They then made further read-only requests using the same public key that the site itself exposes.

Records containing email addresses appeared in 10,560 tables across 7,403 sites, about 30% of the checked set. The exposed data included profiles with birth dates, chat messages, ticket and food sale records with payment details, AI summaries of internal emails, contracts, and over 1,000 records with passport numbers and nationalities. One provider exposed 280,000 emails sent to its customers.

The authors are careful about limits. Email addresses are only a proxy, so 30% is not a confirmed leak rate, and the sample is not representative of all Lovable apps. The report ties the problem to recurring access-control mistakes in database integrations and notes that the platform's terms put security on the customer while its marketing suggests no technical skill is needed. They recommend a review of permissions and user separation before real data goes in, and a professional assessment rather than automated checks alone.
takeaways: The weakness is access control, not a clever exploit: data was readable by anyone who could load the site.
A key that ships to the browser is public by design, so the database must enforce who can read which rows.
Studying public web archives let the researchers survey a whole ecosystem without attacking individual targets.
Recurring mistake patterns mean one approach can work across thousands of apps.
Easy app builders move security responsibility to people who may not know it exists.
An email address is a handy but imperfect proxy for personal data, so honest reports state their limits.
The researchers kept to read-only requests and withheld access details, which is a model for responsible research.
Automated checks help but do not replace a human review of permissions.

terms.name: Chat Messages
terms.text: Adversaries may directly collect unsecured credentials stored or passed through user communication services. Credentials may be sent and stored in user chat communication applications such as email, chat services like Slack or Teams, collaboration tools like Jira or Trello, and any other services that support user communication.

terms.name: Email Addresses
terms.text: Adversaries may gather email addresses that can be used during targeting. Even if internal instances exist, organizations may have public-facing email infrastructure and addresses for employees.

items.title: Lovable apps expose passport details and more than 200K private messages
items.why: It shows, at internet scale, how a missing access-control check in AI-generated apps leaks real personal data, and it is easy to follow without deep expertise.

practice: On a machine you own, review your security product's logs and list every file it reported submitting, then judge whether each was something you meant to share.
Use a packet-capture tool on your own computer for 15 minutes and group traffic by process and destination to see what talks to whom.
Read the vendor documentation for the sample submission consent levels and write down what each level sends.
Check whether a privacy setting you changed earlier is still in place a day or a week later, and keep a log of the results.
Write a short policy for a development laptop covering telemetry, sample submission and where build output lives.

questions.answer: They were troubleshooting a slow connection and saw large uploads from Defender's command-line component in their per-process traffic tool.
questions.question: What first led the author to notice the uploads?

questions.answer: The Defender Operational log, Event 2050, listing what was submitted.
questions.question: Which log records Defender's sample submissions?

questions.answer: Many services use that storage, so the traffic has to be matched to Defender's event entries to confirm it.
questions.question: Why is a connection to Azure storage not proof of a sample upload?

questions.answer: No uploads were logged while disabled, but the setting returned to "send" about two hours later with no action they could identify.
questions.question: What happened when the author disabled sample submission?

questions.answer: It gives control over uploads but also disables block-at-first-sight based on sample analysis, reducing some protection.
questions.question: What is the trade-off of disabling automatic sample submission?

items.summary:
The author built Hodometer, a Windows tray tool that tracks network traffic per process and destination. While chasing a slow connection, they noticed large uploads from Microsoft Defender's command-line component. Defender's Operational log showed 217 sample submissions (Event 2050) over three months, none with a consent prompt that the author remembered. Most were builds of a Go test program they kept rebuilding, but 16 were unreleased programs, and others were a Python script from the Recycle Bin and a temporary database file. One day alone saw about 224 MB uploaded.

An AI agent, with the author's approval, connected to Hodometer's local socket and correlated process history with Defender's logs, per-app data usage records and connection audit. The author also found that turning off sample submission reverted to "send" about two hours later, and that disabling the main telemetry service did not stop other Microsoft components from connecting. Defender's support log held 85 entries with full command lines that included user and project folder names.

The author argues that Defender's default of sending "safe" samples treats a low chance of personal data as consent, which they dispute for unreleased work. No Microsoft response is reported. The piece stresses that a connection to cloud storage alone proves nothing, so traffic must be matched to event logs, and that turning off sample submission also reduces some protection.
takeaways: Security products themselves send data out, so endpoint monitoring should include them.
Event 2050 in Defender's operational log lists sample submissions and the file paths involved.
Correlating per-process network traffic with application logs is stronger evidence than traffic volume alone.
Build output folders on developer machines are a likely place for unintended uploads.
Settings can silently revert, so verify them over time rather than trusting a single change.
Disabling a telemetry service does not guarantee other components stop connecting.
Turning off sample submission has a defensive cost, including weaker block-at-first-sight.
Support logs can hold command lines with usernames and project names, which is a privacy consideration.
items.title: Caught Microsoft Red-Handed with Hodometer
items.why: It is a concrete example of auditing your own endpoint's outbound traffic and security-tool logs to find out what a trusted defender product really sends out.

practice: Read the ZIP file format specification and sketch on paper where each local header field sits and which could hold other values.
In an emulator you control, read how a BIOS boot sector is loaded and what the signature check looks like.
Study the Multiboot specification and note what a loader expects to find in a kernel image.
Write a plain-language table of 8086 opcodes that act as harmless filler and explain why they are safe.
Open an archive in a hex viewer and label the header, entry data and central directory by hand.

questions.answer: ZIP readers find entries through the central directory at the end, so many tolerate unusual or arbitrary data before the first entry.
questions.question: Why can a ZIP file carry extra bytes at the front?

questions.answer: Its magic and field values were chosen so they decode as harmless x86 instructions, with the timestamp field holding a jump over the rest of the header.
questions.question: How does the first header work as both ZIP and code?

questions.answer: It loads 512 bytes and checks for a boot signature at the end of the sector before running the code.
questions.question: What does the BIOS require of the first sector?

questions.answer: It lets QEMU's direct kernel boot treat the file as a Multiboot kernel.
questions.question: What role does the Multiboot magic number play?

questions.answer: Detect the CPU, enable A20, read disk geometry and the archive, detect memory, and enter unreal mode.
questions.question: What are some jobs of the boot code before reaching protected mode?

items.summary:
The author built a file that is a valid ZIP archive and also boots on x86 hardware. It opens normally in an unzip tool, and it boots in QEMU, from a floppy image or hard drive, and on real vintage machines. The trick relies on the ZIP local file header, which starts with a fixed magic value followed by small fields. Because ZIP readers locate entries through a directory at the end, the format tolerates unusual content, and the author picked header values that also decode as harmless 8086 instructions. The magic bytes become a stack push, version and flag fields become benign opcodes, the compression method is set to stored, and the timestamp field holds a short relative jump into the real boot code. A Multiboot magic number placed after the header lets QEMU's direct kernel boot load it as well.

The BIOS loads the first 512 bytes and checks a signature at the end of that sector, so the same bytes must satisfy both an archiver and the CPU. Some modern archivers that scan from the front reject files with gaps, so the archive must begin directly with a local header.

The boot code does a lot in about 817 bytes including headers and the descriptor table: it detects the CPU without CPUID, enables the A20 line by several fallback methods, reads disk geometry and loads the rest of the archive through BIOS calls, probes memory by several interfaces, enters unreal mode, then moves to 32-bit protected mode and jumps to the Multiboot entry, which finds the files inside its own memory image. The result contains its own source and build script, and was tested on a Pentium MMX, an i486 DX2 and an Am386DX-40.
takeaways: A polyglot file works when one set of bytes satisfies two different parsers at once.
ZIP is read from the end, which leaves room at the front for content other tools treat as data.
Header fields can be chosen so they also decode as harmless CPU instructions.
A short relative jump in a spare field can skip over the rest of a header into real code.
BIOS boot expects a 512-byte first sector with a signature at its end, which constrains the layout.
Multiboot support lets emulators load the same file without a separate boot path.
Real mode boot code must handle old hardware differences, such as CPUs without CPUID and varied A20 methods.
Understanding format polyglots also helps defenders see how parsers can be confused.
items.title: Creating a self booting ZIP archive
items.why: It is a rare, hands-on look at how two file formats and the x86 boot process can be made to overlap in a single file.

practice: Read the documentation on how your framework seeds its random number generator and write down which settings could change the output across devices.
Compare the first values of a small randomly initialized layer on two environments you control and note when they differ.
Work out on paper how many parameter combinations a search space of a given size has, and what sigma threshold keeps false matches negligible.
Write a short critique of the report listing three alternative explanations and what evidence would separate them.
Read about how floating-point rounding differs across hardware and list where that could leave traces in your own numerical code.

questions.answer: The streaming-multiprocessor count changes how the random-number work is split across threads, which changes where generated values land.
questions.question: What property of GPUs makes this fingerprint possible?

questions.answer: They receive little or no training, so they keep their initial values almost exactly and preserve the clearest trace.
questions.question: Why are unused vocabulary rows useful?

questions.answer: They set an 8 sigma threshold for the six trillion combinations searched, selected settings on some weights and tested on held-out weights.
questions.question: How did the author guard against false matches?

questions.answer: It matched 24 models with publicly disclosed hardware and reproduced values on rented H100, B300 and GB200 machines.
questions.question: How was the method validated?

questions.answer: It does not show where the chips were, how they were obtained, or whether export controls were broken, and initialization hardware may differ from training hardware.
questions.question: What does the report not establish?

items.summary:
The report argues that six recent models from four Chinese labs (DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax and Ant Group) were initialized on NVIDIA Blackwell-class GPUs, while their earlier models match the older Hopper generation. The core idea is that PyTorch generates starting weights with a pseudorandom generator in NVIDIA's cuRAND library, and the number of streaming multiprocessors on the GPU decides how work is split across threads and so where values land. Hopper has 132, B200 and B300 have 148, and GB200 and GB300 have 152. The author searches for the seed and thread layout that reproduce surviving initial values, such as unused vocabulary rows that stay almost unchanged, with weaker traces in trained weights.

Validation is thorough. Combinations are chosen on one set of weights and tested on held-out ones. Matches are reported at 49 to 1,385 sigma against a roughly 8 sigma chance threshold across about six trillion combinations. The method was checked on 24 models whose hardware was publicly disclosed, and on rented H100, B300 and GB200 machines. AMD MI300X can mimic some layouts, but rounding evidence favors NVIDIA. The author estimates about 12,000 Blackwell GPUs across five runs, with a wide range.

The limits are stated plainly. It works only on published weights and frameworks that leave a hardware-dependent pattern. Some Qwen models, ERNIE-5.5 and LongCat-2.0 gave no signature. It shows where initialization happened, not necessarily all training, cannot separate H800, H100 and H200, and does not show how chips were obtained or whether rules were broken.
takeaways: Pseudorandom initialization can leave a hardware-dependent trace that survives into released weights.
The GPU's multiprocessor count shapes how random numbers are laid out, which acts as a fingerprint.
Parts of a model that are barely trained, like unused vocabulary rows, keep the cleanest evidence.
Fit on one set of weights and test on held-out weights to avoid fooling yourself.
Calibrating on models with publicly known hardware shows whether the method is reliable.
Sigma values only mean something next to the number of combinations searched.
Rule out alternatives, such as AMD hardware that mimics layouts, before concluding.
Detecting initialization hardware does not prove where or how training ran or how chips were acquired.
items.title: Top Chinese Frontier AI Models Carry the Fingerprint of Export-Controlled NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs
items.why: It is a clever piece of forensics that recovers hardware details from the leftover random initialization in published model weights, with careful validation and stated limits.

practice: Map your own organization's or home lab's patch process and write down how many days pass between a vendor fix and your installation.
Pick a public advisory with a patch and read the fix notes to see how much the change reveals about the bug.
Draft a short response plan for a bug that becomes public before a fix exists, listing non-patch mitigations you could apply in a test environment.
Read the previous Project Zero policy posts and compare their stated goals with the new ones.
Build a simple tracking sheet of the software you run and the days each vendor typically takes to ship fixes.

questions.answer: It gave vendors 90 days to fix a bug plus 30 days of soak time before details were published.
questions.question: What did the old policy look like?

questions.answer: Full 90 now, Full 60 from February 2, 2027, and Full 30 from January 3, 2028.
questions.question: What are the new deadlines?

questions.answer: Attackers can work out bug details from a patch almost immediately, so waiting after a fix creates a false sense of secrecy.
questions.question: Why does the team say soak time offers little protection?

questions.answer: Severity affects user impact, not how easily attackers can find a bug.
questions.question: Why is severity not used for disclosure decisions?

questions.answer: Actively exploited bugs, publicly known bugs at the team's discretion, and vendor requests to publish details.
questions.question: What exceptions remain?

items.summary:
Since 2021 Project Zero used a "90 + 30" policy: 90 days for a vendor to fix a bug, then 30 days of soak time for rollout. The new policy, called "Full X", discloses every bug a fixed number of days after it is reported, and that number shrinks. It is Full 90 as of November 13, 2026, Full 60 from February 2, 2027, and Full 30 from January 3, 2028. Most special cases, including the grace period and variant policy, are removed. Three exceptions remain: actively exploited bugs follow Google's application security policy, publicly known bugs may be disclosed at the team's discretion, and vendor requests to publish details are honored.

The reasoning has four parts. AI-assisted discovery and exploitation make bugs easier to find and more likely to be found by several parties at once. Patches reveal bugs, since attackers can work out details almost immediately, so soak time gives little protection. The patch gap, the time between a fix and its installation, should be closed by faster rollout or other protections. And the team now finds several bugs a week, so negotiating each one is unmanageable.

The phased schedule responds to vendor worries about exposing unfixed bugs and about prioritizing by deadline rather than severity. Severity is not used to decide disclosure, since it affects impact, not how findable a bug is. Hardware vendors are asked to plan for imminent disclosure with non-patch mitigations, and fix tracking continues but no longer triggers policy decisions.
takeaways: The disclosure clock is now a fixed number of days from report, with no extra soak or grace periods.
The deadline steps down from 90 to 60 days in early 2027 and 30 days in 2028.
AI tools make parallel discovery and fast patch analysis more likely, which weakens secrecy.
A published patch effectively discloses the bug, so the patch gap is the real exposure window.
Disclosure timing ignores severity, because findability does not depend on it.
Actively exploited bugs, publicly known bugs and vendor requests remain exceptions.
Defenders need faster patch rollout and non-patch mitigations rather than relying on delay.
A gradual schedule gives vendors time to adapt their processes.
items.title: Project Zero will disclose vulnerabilities 90 days after reporting
items.why: It explains why a leading research team is shortening disclosure deadlines in the age of AI-assisted bug finding and patch diffing, which affects every defender's patching plans.
